The Singleton Pattern Is Simple, But Not Innocent The Singleton pattern is one of the most recognizable design patterns in object-oriented programming, and also one of the most misunderstood.
At its core, the Singleton pattern guarantees that a class has exactly one instance and provides a global access point to it. In Java, this is usually used for runtime configuration, shared caches, thread pools, logging, or application-wide coordination.
Sounds straightforward, right?
The problem is that “single instance” is often treated as a solution in search of a problem. In real systems, global state is a trade-off. It is convenient, but it often introduces hidden coupling, makes testing harder, and can become an accidental bottleneck when the system grows.
The Singleton pattern is useful when it represents a true application-level concept, not when it is used as a shortcut to avoid passing dependencies around.
That distinction matters.
What the Singleton Pattern Is Trying to Solve The Singleton pattern addresses a specific problem: some objects should exist only once in a running environment because the system depends on a single source of truth.
Examples:
a configuration manager a process-wide logger a shared connection factory a registry of application services a cache that must stay consistent across the JVM The pattern enforces a single instance and centralizes access to it.
This is attractive because it reduces duplication and makes lifecycle management explicit. But it also means the object becomes part of the system’s global state. That can be a strength or a liability depending on the design.
A good rule: use a Singleton only when the object truly represents a single runtime concern, not just because it is convenient to keep everything accessible from one place.
The Classical Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four describes Singleton as a pattern that ensures a class has one instance and provides a global point of access.
In practice, that usually means:
the constructor is private or otherwise restricted a static method returns the single instance the instance is created lazily or eagerly depending on the strategy The key idea is to control object creation so the application has a single consistent instance.
From an architecture perspective, the Singleton pattern is best understood as a lifecycle management pattern, not as a substitute for proper dependency design.
A Simple Java Example: Eager Initialization Here is the most straightforward version of the Singleton pattern in Java:
public class AppConfig { private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig(); private final String environment; private AppConfig() { this.environment = System.getenv().getOrDefault("APP_ENV", "dev"); } public static AppConfig getInstance() { return INSTANCE; } public String getEnvironment() { return environment; } } This is easy to reason about. The instance is created when the class loads, which makes it thread-safe by default.
The downside is that it may create an object eagerly even when the application does not use it. In many cases, that is acceptable. For configuration or logging, it often is.
But in larger systems, eager initialization can be wasteful or can trigger expensive work too early.
Lazy Initialization If you want to create the instance only when it is first needed, you can use lazy initialization:
public class AppConfig { private static AppConfig instance; private AppConfig() { } public static synchronized AppConfig getInstance() { if (instance == null) { instance = new AppConfig(); } return instance; } } This version avoids creating the object up front, but it uses synchronized on every access. That makes it thread-safe, though it introduces overhead.
For a system that is heavily read during normal operation, that performance cost can become noticeable.
Double-Checked Locking A more efficient thread-safe approach is double-checked locking:
public class AppConfig { private static volatile AppConfig instance; private AppConfig() { } public static AppConfig getInstance() { if (instance == null) { synchronized (AppConfig.class) { if (instance == null) { instance = new AppConfig(); } } } return instance; } } This version minimizes locking overhead while still ensuring safe publication. The use of volatile is important because it prevents stale reads and reordering issues.
This is a classic Java pattern for lazy-singleton initialization. It is still widely discussed, but there is usually an even cleaner alternative.
The Best Java Idiom: Initialization-on-Demand Holder The most common production-safe pattern in Java today is the initialization-on-demand holder idiom:
public class AppConfig { private AppConfig() { } private static class Holder { private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig(); } public static AppConfig getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } This pattern is elegant because:
it is lazy it is thread-safe it avoids synchronization overhead it is simple to understand Java will initialize the nested class only when getInstance() is called. This is often the best choice for a JVM-based service that needs a single instance and no extra ceremony.
This is the kind of implementation I would typically keep in a real enterprise codebase when a true singleton is justified.
When a Singleton Makes Sense A Singleton is appropriate when one instance truly represents a single runtime resource or process-wide policy.
Common examples:
public class MetricsRegistry { private static final MetricsRegistry INSTANCE = new MetricsRegistry(); private final Map<String, Long> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private MetricsRegistry() { } public static MetricsRegistry getInstance() { return INSTANCE; } public void increment(String metricName) { counters.merge(metricName, 1L, Long::sum); } } This is reasonable because a metrics registry is a process-wide concern. A single registry keeps all metrics aggregation centralized.
Another example is a configuration object:
public class EnvironmentConfig { private static class Holder { private static final EnvironmentConfig INSTANCE = new EnvironmentConfig(); } private final String apiBaseUrl; private EnvironmentConfig() { this.apiBaseUrl = System.getenv().getOrDefault("API_BASE_URL", "http://localhost:8080"); } public static EnvironmentConfig getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } public String getApiBaseUrl() { return apiBaseUrl; } } This is a good example of a singleton representing a true application-wide configuration, not just a convenient holder for random state.
When the Singleton Pattern Becomes a Problem This is where engineering judgment matters.
The Singleton pattern is easy to overuse, and when it is used poorly it creates hidden global state. That introduces several problems:
1. It hides dependencies If a class depends on a singleton, it is not obvious from the constructor what it needs to function.
public class PaymentService { public void processPayment() { PaymentGateway gateway = PaymentGateway.getInstance(); gateway.charge(100); } } This makes the class harder to test and reason about because the dependency is not explicit.
2. It makes unit testing harder Singletons are hard to replace with test doubles. In many codebases, this leads to brittle tests or broad mocking setups.
3. It creates global coupling When many components reach into a singleton, the system becomes more tightly connected than it appears on the surface.
4. It can become a concurrency bottleneck If the singleton owns shared mutable state, everything touches the same object and contention increases.
This does not mean Singletons are always wrong. It means they should be used deliberately and only where the lifecycle semantics justify it.
A Better Alternative in Many Cases: Dependency Injection In modern Java applications, the preferred pattern is often to inject dependencies explicitly rather than reaching into global state.
public class PaymentService { private final PaymentGateway paymentGateway; public PaymentService(PaymentGateway paymentGateway) { this.paymentGateway = paymentGateway; } public void processPayment() { paymentGateway.charge(100); } } This is easier to test, easier to reason about, and more explicit about the object’s runtime relationships.
In a Spring application, this is usually the preferred model. A singleton-like service can still be configured as a bean, but the dependency graph remains explicit.
The Singleton pattern is not inherently bad. It is just often less desirable than explicit wiring when the real requirement is not a global singleton at all.
The Enum Singleton in Java If a class truly needs to be a singleton, the safest Java-specific implementation is often an enum singleton:
public enum SecurityContext { INSTANCE; private final String currentUser = "system"; public String getCurrentUser() { return currentUser; } } This is a strong option because:
the JVM guarantees only one instance exists serialization is handled safely thread safety is built in reflection-based attacks are much harder to execute This is usually the most robust approach when you truly need a singleton in Java.
The trade-off is that an enum is a bit more opinionated. It only makes sense when the singleton is conceptually a fixed, process-wide value or service.
Practical Guidance for Real Teams Here is how I think about the Singleton pattern in production systems:
Use it for true process-wide resources that are conceptually singular. Avoid it for ordinary business objects or convenience access. Prefer explicit dependency injection whenever the object is not truly global. Keep the singleton stateless or carefully controlled when possible. Be careful with mutable shared state. If you use a singleton, choose a thread-safe implementation and document the reason. A good mental model is: a Singleton is an architecture decision, not a coding shortcut.
Final Thoughts The Singleton pattern is one of the clearest examples of a design pattern that is simple to explain and easy to misuse.
Its value is real when you need a single, well-defined runtime authority: a configuration hub, a metrics registry, a process-wide coordination object, or a service that must be globally consistent.
Its risk is equally real when it becomes a hidden global variable in disguise.
That is why the Singleton pattern deserves respect, but not worship.
The right question is not “Can I make this a singleton?” The better question is “Does the system truly require exactly one instance, and does that design improve correctness and maintainability rather than merely reducing typing?”
That is the difference between an intentional design and a convenience hack.
If you want a singleton, implement it carefully. If you do not need one, avoid it. The best Java code is usually the code that makes its dependencies explicit and keeps the system honest.

Design Patterns Are Not a Fancy Acronym. They Are a Professional Discipline. When I review code, the difference between a team that is shipping features and a team that is building durable systems is usually not raw intelligence. It is the discipline of design.
The best engineering teams do not treat design as a luxury. They treat it as a force multiplier.
Design patterns are one of the clearest expressions of that discipline. They are not “pattern matching” for the sake of aesthetics. They are battle-tested ways to structure code so that software is easier to understand, easier to extend, and less likely to collapse under the weight of change.
In enterprise Java systems, where requirements evolve, integrations multiply, and technical debt accumulates quietly over time, patterns matter even more. A team that understands design patterns usually writes software that is more coherent, easier to test, and less likely to require a rewrite after the second or third major release.
The real question is not whether you know the names of the patterns. The question is whether you know when to apply them and whether you can apply them without over-engineering.
That is the difference between a clever engineer and a principal engineer.
Why Design Patterns Matter in Software Engineering Software engineering is fundamentally about managing complexity.
Every system starts with a clean idea and a plausible code path. Then real life arrives: new requirements, changing data sources, regulatory constraints, third-party APIs, performance problems, and the inevitable pressure to patch quickly. That is when complexity becomes the real adversary.
Design patterns help by giving us a vocabulary for recurring problems.
Instead of every developer inventing a custom solution from scratch, a mature team can say:
“This is a strategy problem.” “This is a factory problem.” “This is a decorator problem.” “This is an observer problem.” That shared language reduces ambiguity. It also helps teams avoid the anti-pattern of doing everything ad hoc and then pretending the lack of structure is a feature.
A pattern is valuable when it does three things well:
It makes intent explicit. It reduces accidental complexity. It supports extensibility without destroying cohesion. Consider a common enterprise scenario: payment processing. If every service in the system calculates fees, builds different gateway clients, and directly couples to vendor classes, the code will become brittle. When a new payment method arrives, the team will edit three or four unrelated classes and the risk of bugs goes up dramatically.
That is exactly the kind of problem design patterns are designed to solve.
The Gang of Four: The Foundation of Modern Object-Oriented Design The book most engineers mean when they say “design patterns” is Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, published in 1994 by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides — collectively known as the Gang of Four, or GoF.
The book changed software engineering by codifying what experienced designers already knew: many object-oriented problems recur, and reusable solutions can be captured and taught.
The GoF did not invent the idea of design patterns in the abstract, but they gave the practice a common language and a durable framework. They organized patterns into three categories:
1. Creational patterns These focus on object creation. They help decouple a system from the concrete classes it creates.
Typical examples:
Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder Singleton Prototype Why they matter:
They control how objects are created. They reduce coupling to constructors and concrete implementations. They make it easier to swap implementations without rewriting the system. 2. Structural patterns These explain how classes and objects compose to form larger structures.
Typical examples:
Adapter Bridge Composite Decorator Facade Flyweight Proxy Why they matter:
They help combine components in a stable way. They let systems evolve without forcing a redesign of the whole object graph. They isolate change behind well-defined boundaries. 3. Behavioral patterns These define communication and responsibility between objects.
Typical examples:
Strategy Observer Command Iterator State Template Method Visitor Why they matter:
They simplify interactions between collaborators. They help distribute responsibilities without producing a tangled object graph. They improve system flexibility when user behavior or workflow changes. The GoF’s core point is simple but powerful: software design is not only about data structures. It is also about the relationships between objects and the responsibilities those objects hold.
That is the real value of the book: it gives engineers a disciplined vocabulary for describing and solving recurring architecture problems.
A Practical Summary of the GoF Book If I had to reduce the book to a single sentence, it would be this:
“Design patterns are reusable object-oriented solutions to recurring design problems, expressed in terms of responsibilities, interactions, and trade-offs.”
This is important because patterns are not magical formulas. They are ways of thinking.
The GoF explicitly frames patterns in terms of:
the problem being solved, the context in which it arises, the participants involved, the consequences of the solution, and the trade-offs you accept. That last point matters more than most people realize. Every pattern makes some aspects of the system easier while making other things more complex. There is no free lunch in architecture.
For example:
A Factory pattern hides construction details, but adds another layer of indirection. A Strategy pattern enables runtime flexibility, but requires a consistent interface across algorithms. A Decorator pattern keeps things open for extension, but can make debugging harder when many wrappers exist. A Singleton pattern is simple to reason about in some cases, but it often becomes a global variable in disguise. The GoF’s value is not that every pattern must be used everywhere. Their value is that they give you a mental model for recognizing the right tool for the right problem.
Good engineers do not memorize patterns. They understand the forces behind them.
The Relationship Between SOLID and Design Patterns If design patterns are the “how,” then SOLID is the “why.”
SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles introduced by Robert C. Martin, and it maps directly to the realities that patterns address.
The five principles are:
Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) A class should have one reason to change.
This principle is the foundation of good cohesion. If a class owns too many responsibilities, it becomes a fragile dependency magnet.
A classic sign of SRP violation is a service that handles validation, persistence, workflow orchestration, and email notifications all in one class.
public class OrderService { public void placeOrder(Order order) { validate(order); save(order); sendConfirmationEmail(order); publishOrderCreatedEvent(order); } private void validate(Order order) { } private void save(Order order) { } private void sendConfirmationEmail(Order order) { } private void publishOrderCreatedEvent(Order order) { } } This class has multiple reasons to change. If email rules change, if persistence changes, or if the order validation model changes, this one class has to be reopened repeatedly.
A more disciplined design splits responsibilities across components.
public class OrderService { private final OrderValidator validator; private final OrderRepository repository; private final OrderNotifier notifier; public OrderService(OrderValidator validator, OrderRepository repository, OrderNotifier notifier) { this.validator = validator; this.repository = repository; this.notifier = notifier; } public void placeOrder(Order order) { validator.validate(order); repository.save(order); notifier.sendConfirmation(order); } } This is not just cleaner code. It is more stable code.
Open/Closed Principle (OCP) Software entities should be open for extension and closed for modification.
This is one of the most important ideas behind patterns like Strategy, Decorator, and Factory. You want to add behavior by introducing new types, not by changing old code in place.
public interface ShippingStrategy { double calculateCost(Order order); } public class GroundShipping implements ShippingStrategy { @Override public double calculateCost(Order order) { return 12.00; } } public class ExpressShipping implements ShippingStrategy { @Override public double calculateCost(Order order) { return 25.00; } } Now the shipping logic can vary without rewriting the order flow:
public class OrderService { private final ShippingStrategy shippingStrategy; public OrderService(ShippingStrategy shippingStrategy) { this.shippingStrategy = shippingStrategy; } public double calculateTotal(Order order) { return order.getSubtotal() + shippingStrategy.calculateCost(order); } } This is an example of the Strategy pattern in action. The behavior is extended by new implementations, not by modifying the order service itself.
Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking the system.
This principle matters whenever we rely on polymorphism. If a subtype violates the expectations of the parent type, the design becomes brittle and surprising.
A classic violation would be using a Square that breaks Rectangle expectations, or a PaymentGateway implementation that throws on refund() because it was only designed for charges.
public interface PaymentGateway { void charge(BigDecimal amount); void refund(BigDecimal amount); } public class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { @Override public void charge(BigDecimal amount) { // charge with Stripe API } @Override public void refund(BigDecimal amount) { // refund with Stripe API } } If a different implementation is added, it should honor the same contract. If it cannot, the abstraction is wrong or too broad.
Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
This leads to small, focused interfaces instead of one “god” interface with dozens of methods.
public interface UserRepository { User findById(String id); void save(User user); } public interface AuditRepository { void recordAudit(AuditEvent event); } Rather than a single bloated interface like UserService and AuditService combined, the design keeps contracts specialized. This reduces coupling and makes implementation easier to maintain.
Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) Depend on abstractions, not concretions.
This principle is critical for enterprise Java systems and is deeply connected to design patterns like Factory, Dependency Injection, and Strategy.
public interface NotificationSender { void send(String message); } public class EmailNotificationSender implements NotificationSender { @Override public void send(String message) { System.out.println("Sending email: " + message); } } Then the client depends on the abstraction:
public class AccountService { private final NotificationSender notificationSender; public AccountService(NotificationSender notificationSender) { this.notificationSender = notificationSender; } public void register(String email) { // business logic notificationSender.send("Welcome!"); } } This is a cleaner design because the service is not hardwired to a specific email provider or implementation detail.
How SOLID Relates to Design Patterns The easiest way to think about this is:
SOLID gives you the principles. Design patterns give you the application of those principles in recurring situations. The relationship is not accidental. Patterns often emerge because a team is trying to satisfy one or more SOLID goals.
Take Strategy as an example.
The goal is to keep behavior extensible and avoid hardcoding logic into a central class. That aligns directly with OCP and DIP. The pattern is the structural expression of those principles in a reusable form.
Similarly:
Factory and Abstract Factory are solutions to construction problems that reduce direct dependency on concrete classes. Decorator is a natural expression of OCP: extend behavior without changing the original type. Observer is a way to manage change propagation while keeping coupling manageable. Facade simplifies a complex system and clarifies boundaries, helping reduce SRP violations from a consumer’s perspective. Adapter helps integrate incompatible interfaces without redesigning the world. A simple rule of thumb:
If SOLID is the architectural compass, design patterns are the map. They guide implementation choices without replacing judgment.
This is where many engineers stumble: they confuse “knowing patterns” with “designing well.” A pattern is not a substitute for thinking. It is a tool to avoid poor thinking.
Patterns Are a Language, Not a Religion I have seen teams over-apply patterns. They create abstract factories for everything, decorate every object, and turn a simple service into a cathedral of indirection.
That is not engineering. It is pattern worship without judgment.
The right standard is not “Do I know a pattern for this?” The right standard is “Does this design reduce uncertainty and clarify intent in a way that helps the next engineer safely evolve the code?”
The best use of design patterns is selective and pragmatic:
Use them where the problem is recurring and the cost of a custom solution is high. Keep the abstraction honest and narrow. Prefer clear behavior over theoretical elegance. Favor simplicity until complexity demonstrates it is necessary. A good design does not impress by showing off. It demonstrates restraint, clarity, and resilience under change.
That is why the GoF patterns endure. They are not just intellectual curiosities. They are practical, repeatable solutions to ordinary engineering problems.
And their value is multiplied when they are grounded in SOLID principles. Patterns without principles become decorative. Principles without patterns become vague philosophy. Together, they form a disciplined approach to building software that can evolve without falling apart.
Final Thoughts Design patterns matter because software engineering is not just about writing code that works once. It is about writing code that remains understandable, flexible, and correct as the system grows.
The Gang of Four distilled the experience of generations of software designers into a toolkit for recurring problems. SOLID principles gave us the underlying guidance for keeping systems coherent and maintainable. Together, they define how thoughtful engineers create software that scales beyond the original sprint.
If you are building in Java, or any language for that matter, the practical takeaway is straightforward:
Notice the recurring design problems. Choose the right pattern for the forces at play. Keep the design aligned with SOLID principles. Refactor toward clarity, not complexity. That is how we move from writing code to engineering systems.
And that is the difference between building features and building software that lasts.

Background Years ago, I started my development journey learning javascript, NodeJS and React. My first project was, like others, building a Pokedex App using the PokeAPI. The architecture was pretty simple:
The UI ran with vanilla javascript and React 15 The backend was a REST API build with NodeJS and Express The database was a flat json file that was basically the same schema as the PokeAPI contract The database was populated by a batch job that fetched the first generation of pokemon flowchart TD UI["React Pokedex UI"] API["Node.js Pokemon API"] DB["JSON Pokemon Database"] BATCH["Batch Job (Fetches Gen 1 Pokémon)"] UI --> API API --> DB BATCH --> DB Since then, there have been many new frameworks and enhancements made in the javascript community that would put my code then to shame. So, in honor of it being nearly 10 years since I did this humble project, I’ve decided to recreate this nostalgic Pokedex app!
Application Design Frontend For the UI, I’ll continue to use React but this time leverage the NextJS framework.
Backend While NextJS supports running it’s own server, I’ll choose to create a dedicated REST API with NodeJS but this time leverage Fastify
Database For my database, I’ll trade in a flat JSON file in favor of first-class datastore in Postgres which supports storing JSON in tables
Eventing Finally to hydrate the database, I will leverage the BullMQ framework to create a lightweight job orchestration process to ingest pokemon data from the PokeAPI
Infrastructure Finally, to help keep my app portable, I will containerize these components using docker and leverage docker compose to orchestrate the communication between the apps
🚧 Stay tuned here for project updates!

Why I Started This Blog As engineers, we spend a lot of time building, experimenting, and solving problems. But too often, those lessons stay hidden inside project folders, Slack threads, or our own heads.
Starting this blog was my way to change that — to document my projects, share what I learn, and hopefully inspire others to build cool things.
1. Document Projects Writing about a project forces you to clarify your thinking. It’s easy to move on to the next shiny idea, but documentation helps future-you (and others) revisit, maintain, and extend your work.
2. Share Knowledge Every engineer learns differently, and your perspective might be the one that helps someone finally understand a tricky concept. Sharing knowledge strengthens the community and makes tech more accessible.
3. Inspire Builders We all got into this field because we love building. When I read other engineers’ blogs, I get inspired to try new stacks, frameworks, or even just better ways of thinking. I hope this blog does the same for someone else.
How I Built This Blog: Hugo + GitHub Pages If you’ve been thinking about starting your own tech blog, you can do it in an afternoon. Here’s the path I took to get this one up and running.
Step 1: Install Hugo Hugo is a static site generator written in Go. It’s fast, flexible, and perfect for developer blogs.
# for mac brew install hugo # or for Windows choco install hugo-extended Check your install:
hugo version Step 2: Create a New Site hugo new site my-tech-blog cd my-tech-blog Step 3: Add a Theme Pick a theme you like from themes.gohugo.io.
Example:
git submodule add https://github.com/adityatelange/hugo-PaperMod echo 'theme = "PaperMod"' >> hugo.toml Step 4: Add Your First Post hugo new posts/your-awesome-post.md Open the file in your editor, write your first post and save.
Step 5: Test Locally hugo server Then visit http://localhost:1313 to preview your blog.
Step 6: Push to GitHub Initialize a repo and push:
git init git add . git commit -m "Initial commit" git branch -M main git remote add origin https://github.com/yourusername/my-tech-blog.git git push -u origin main Step 7: Deploy with GitHub Pages You can deploy using a GitHub Actions workflow:
Create .github/workflows/hugo.yml:
name: Build and deploy on: push: branches: - main # Set a branch to deploy pull_request: jobs: deploy: runs-on: ubuntu-24.04 concurrency: group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 with: submodules: true # Fetch Hugo themes (true OR recursive) fetch-depth: 0 # Fetch all history for .GitInfo and .Lastmod - name: Setup Hugo uses: peaceiris/actions-hugo@v3 with: hugo-version: '0.119.0' # extended: true - name: Build run: hugo --minify - name: Deploy uses: peaceiris/actions-gh-pages@v3 if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' with: github_token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} publish_dir: ./public Push the workflow, and your blog will auto-deploy to https://yourusername.github.io/my-tech-blog/.
Final Thoughts Blogging as a developer isn’t just about writing — it’s about creating a living record of your journey.
It’s a way to give back, stay accountable, and connect with others who love to build.
If you’ve ever thought, “I should start a blog,” — take this as your nudge.
Start small, share your process, and let others learn alongside you.
Happy building!

As engineers, we spend a lot of time building, experimenting, and solving problems. But too often, those lessons stay hidden inside project folders, Slack threads, or our own heads.

Starting this blog was my way to change that — to document my projects, share what I learn, and hopefully inspire others to build cool things.

1. Document Projects

Writing about a project forces you to clarify your thinking. It’s easy to move on to the next shiny idea, but documentation helps future-you (and others) revisit, maintain, and extend your work.
title: Why I Started a Tech Blog (and How You Can Too with Hugo + GitHub Pages)

The Abstract Factory Pattern Solves a Specific Design Problem The Singleton pattern is about one instance. The Abstract Factory pattern is about families of related objects.
That difference matters.
If you are building software that must work across multiple implementations of a common domain, a simple factory may be enough. But when the system needs to create a set of related products together—such as a UI toolkit, a database access layer, or a messaging stack—the Abstract Factory pattern gives you a more coherent and extensible abstraction.
This pattern is one of the most useful creational patterns in enterprise Java design because it allows a system to depend on interfaces and families of implementations without becoming tightly coupled to exact classes.
It is also one of the easiest patterns to misuse. The common temptation is to introduce an abstract factory too early, before the domain has enough shape. That creates extra architecture without real payoff. A pattern is only valuable when it solves a real variation problem.
Why Families of Objects Matter Most complex systems depend on multiple related objects working together.
Think about a UI framework:
a button a checkbox a text field a scroll bar These are not just random objects. They are a family of UI components that need to share a visual language and behavior.
Now imagine the same application must support both a desktop theme and a mobile theme. The classes are different, but the interfaces are the same. You do not want client code to know which concrete implementation is being used. You want the client to ask for a factory and then consume the product family through stable interfaces.
That is exactly the problem the Abstract Factory pattern addresses.
The Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four describes the Abstract Factory pattern as a way to provide an interface for creating families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes.
The idea is simple but powerful:
define a product family define a factory interface for creating each product in that family create concrete factories for each implementation family let the client depend on the abstract factory and abstract products, not the concrete variants This keeps the system open for extension and closed for modification. When a new implementation family appears, you add a new concrete factory rather than rewriting every call site.
Abstract Factory vs Factory Method These two patterns are related, but they solve different problems.
Factory Method The Factory Method pattern usually gives you one point of variation: one object is created through a subclass or a method.
Example: a DocumentParserFactory creates a parser for a document type.
Abstract Factory The Abstract Factory pattern is broader. It creates a family of related objects together. Think of it as a higher-level factory, one layer above the individual product factories.
Example: a UIFactory creates a Button, TextField, and Dialog that all belong to the same platform family.
A simple rule:
use Factory Method when you vary one product use Abstract Factory when you vary a whole family of related products If you try to force an abstract factory into a small codebase, you may over-engineer the solution. But in a platform abstraction or cross-environment design, it becomes extremely valuable.
A Java Example: UI Components Across Platforms Let us look at a typical cross-platform scenario.
We want to create desktop and mobile UI components that share a common interface but have different implementations.
Product interfaces public interface Button { void render(); } public interface TextField { void render(); } Concrete products for desktop public class DesktopButton implements Button { @Override public void render() { System.out.println("Rendering desktop button"); } } public class DesktopTextField implements TextField { @Override public void render() { System.out.println("Rendering desktop text field"); } } Concrete products for mobile public class MobileButton implements Button { @Override public void render() { System.out.println("Rendering mobile button"); } } public class MobileTextField implements TextField { @Override public void render() { System.out.println("Rendering mobile text field"); } } Abstract factory public interface UIFactory { Button createButton(); TextField createTextField(); } Concrete factories public class DesktopUIFactory implements UIFactory { @Override public Button createButton() { return new DesktopButton(); } @Override public TextField createTextField() { return new DesktopTextField(); } } public class MobileUIFactory implements UIFactory { @Override public Button createButton() { return new MobileButton(); } @Override public TextField createTextField() { return new MobileTextField(); } } Client code public class LoginForm { private final Button submitButton; private final TextField usernameField; public LoginForm(UIFactory factory) { this.submitButton = factory.createButton(); this.usernameField = factory.createTextField(); } public void render() { usernameField.render(); submitButton.render(); } } Usage public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { UIFactory factory = new DesktopUIFactory(); LoginForm form = new LoginForm(factory); form.render(); } } This is exactly the benefit of the pattern: the client code asks for a family of related objects and does not care whether the actual implementation is desktop or mobile.
A Real-World Example: Payment Providers Another strong example is a payment system that supports multiple providers.
You may need:
a PaymentGateway a RefundProcessor a RiskEvaluator These all belong to a provider family and need to work together as a coherent system.
Interfaces public interface PaymentGateway { void authorize(String userId, double amount); } public interface RefundProcessor { void refund(String paymentId, double amount); } public interface RiskEvaluator { boolean isHighRisk(String userId); } Stripe implementation family public class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { @Override public void authorize(String userId, double amount) { System.out.println("Stripe authorized payment for user " + userId); } } public class StripeRefundProcessor implements RefundProcessor { @Override public void refund(String paymentId, double amount) { System.out.println("Stripe refunded payment " + paymentId); } } public class StripeRiskEvaluator implements RiskEvaluator { @Override public boolean isHighRisk(String userId) { return false; } } PayPal implementation family public class PayPalGateway implements PaymentGateway { @Override public void authorize(String userId, double amount) { System.out.println("PayPal authorized payment for user " + userId); } } public class PayPalRefundProcessor implements RefundProcessor { @Override public void refund(String paymentId, double amount) { System.out.println("PayPal refunded payment " + paymentId); } } public class PayPalRiskEvaluator implements RiskEvaluator { @Override public boolean isHighRisk(String userId) { return true; } } Factory interface public interface PaymentProviderFactory { PaymentGateway createPaymentGateway(); RefundProcessor createRefundProcessor(); RiskEvaluator createRiskEvaluator(); } Concrete factory public class StripeFactory implements PaymentProviderFactory { @Override public PaymentGateway createPaymentGateway() { return new StripeGateway(); } @Override public RefundProcessor createRefundProcessor() { return new StripeRefundProcessor(); } @Override public RiskEvaluator createRiskEvaluator() { return new StripeRiskEvaluator(); } } This pattern becomes valuable when different providers require different implementation details, but the business process expects a consistent contract.
Why the Pattern Is Valuable in Java Systems The Abstract Factory pattern is especially useful when you need to:
support multiple implementations behind one consistent API vary an entire product family without changing client code isolate platform-specific concerns keep the system decoupled from concrete classes It is often used in layered applications where each environment or provider has its own concrete implementation while the rest of the service layer depends only on abstractions.
In Java enterprise code, this is common in:
UI libraries persistence abstractions cloud provider adapters message broker implementations payment and fraud frameworks The pattern helps a system remain maintainable as the number of variants grows. A codebase that hardcodes if (provider == "stripe") all over the place is usually a smell. The Abstract Factory pattern gives a cleaner place to centralize that logic.
The Design Trade-Offs The Abstract Factory pattern is not free.
It adds abstraction. It introduces more types and more indirection. That means a team must justify the additional structure.
The downside is visible when the system is simple and the product family is not actually variant-rich. In a small application, an abstract factory can make the code feel heavier than the problem deserves.
This is where technical judgment matters.
A good design does not add abstraction because it looks “clean.” It adds it because the product families are real and the flexibility is valuable.
If your code only has one implementation and no meaningful variation, an abstract factory is probably unnecessary. If you have multiple platform-specific or provider-specific implementations that must stay consistent, it becomes a strong design choice.
How It Relates to SOLID The Abstract Factory pattern aligns clearly with the SOLID principles, especially the Open/Closed Principle and the Dependency Inversion Principle.
Open/Closed Principle The client code depends on abstractions, not concrete classes. Adding a new factory or product family does not require rewriting the client logic. You add new implementations instead.
Dependency Inversion Principle The system depends on interfaces such as UIFactory, Button, and TextField, not direct classes like DesktopButton or StripeGateway.
This is the same reason the pattern is powerful: it keeps high-level logic independent from low-level decisions.
Single Responsibility Principle The factory is responsible for creating products in a coherent family. The client stays focused on business behavior and delegates creation to the factory.
This pattern is a concrete expression of those principles in a recurring design problem.
A Common Anti-Pattern: Factory Explosion A lot of teams create abstract factories too early and then end up with a forest of abstract types, product interfaces, and implementation classes that never really change.
This is the trap.
The pattern is not a reward for complexity. It is a tool for complexity that is real, recurring, and worth managing.
Before introducing an abstract factory, ask:
are there multiple related families? will these implementations vary over time? do the products need to stay consistent as a set? is the logic likely to accumulate conditional branching if we do not abstract it? If the answer is mostly no, then a simpler factory or direct dependency injection may be a better fit.
Dependency Injection and Abstract Factories Together In modern Java applications, the Abstract Factory pattern often pairs well with dependency injection.
Instead of constructing a factory directly in the client, you can inject it:
public class CheckoutService { private final PaymentProviderFactory paymentProviderFactory; public CheckoutService(PaymentProviderFactory paymentProviderFactory) { this.paymentProviderFactory = paymentProviderFactory; } public void processPayment(String userId, double amount) { PaymentGateway gateway = paymentProviderFactory.createPaymentGateway(); gateway.authorize(userId, amount); } } This keeps the service logic clean and makes the provider selection explicit at the composition root.
This is a good example of how patterns and modern object-oriented design work together. The pattern still matters, but the wiring becomes more explicit and testable.
Final Thoughts The Abstract Factory pattern is a strong solution when a system must work with families of related objects and keep the client code independent from concrete implementation choices.
It is particularly effective when your codebase must support:
multiple platforms multiple providers distinct implementation families consistent object sets that belong together It becomes less valuable when the variation is shallow or the domain is too small to justify the added layers.
The best engineering decisions are not made by memorizing patterns. They are made by recognizing the shape of the problem.
If the system needs a coherent family of related objects, the Abstract Factory pattern is not just elegant—it is practical. If it does not, then simpler abstractions are likely the better choice.
That is the design discipline that separates thoughtful engineering from pattern-heavy complexity.

The Singleton Pattern Is Simple, But Not Innocent The Singleton pattern is one of the most recognizable design patterns in object-oriented programming, and also one of the most misunderstood.
At its core, the Singleton pattern guarantees that a class has exactly one instance and provides a global access point to it. In Java, this is usually used for runtime configuration, shared caches, thread pools, logging, or application-wide coordination.
Sounds straightforward, right?
The problem is that “single instance” is often treated as a solution in search of a problem. In real systems, global state is a trade-off. It is convenient, but it often introduces hidden coupling, makes testing harder, and can become an accidental bottleneck when the system grows.
The Singleton pattern is useful when it represents a true application-level concept, not when it is used as a shortcut to avoid passing dependencies around.
That distinction matters.
What the Singleton Pattern Is Trying to Solve The Singleton pattern addresses a specific problem: some objects should exist only once in a running environment because the system depends on a single source of truth.
Examples:
a configuration manager a process-wide logger a shared connection factory a registry of application services a cache that must stay consistent across the JVM The pattern enforces a single instance and centralizes access to it.
This is attractive because it reduces duplication and makes lifecycle management explicit. But it also means the object becomes part of the system’s global state. That can be a strength or a liability depending on the design.
A good rule: use a Singleton only when the object truly represents a single runtime concern, not just because it is convenient to keep everything accessible from one place.
The Classical Gang of Four Intent The Gang of Four describes Singleton as a pattern that ensures a class has one instance and provides a global point of access.
In practice, that usually means:
the constructor is private or otherwise restricted a static method returns the single instance the instance is created lazily or eagerly depending on the strategy The key idea is to control object creation so the application has a single consistent instance.
From an architecture perspective, the Singleton pattern is best understood as a lifecycle management pattern, not as a substitute for proper dependency design.
A Simple Java Example: Eager Initialization Here is the most straightforward version of the Singleton pattern in Java:
public class AppConfig { private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig(); private final String environment; private AppConfig() { this.environment = System.getenv().getOrDefault("APP_ENV", "dev"); } public static AppConfig getInstance() { return INSTANCE; } public String getEnvironment() { return environment; } } This is easy to reason about. The instance is created when the class loads, which makes it thread-safe by default.
The downside is that it may create an object eagerly even when the application does not use it. In many cases, that is acceptable. For configuration or logging, it often is.
But in larger systems, eager initialization can be wasteful or can trigger expensive work too early.
Lazy Initialization If you want to create the instance only when it is first needed, you can use lazy initialization:
public class AppConfig { private static AppConfig instance; private AppConfig() { } public static synchronized AppConfig getInstance() { if (instance == null) { instance = new AppConfig(); } return instance; } } This version avoids creating the object up front, but it uses synchronized on every access. That makes it thread-safe, though it introduces overhead.
For a system that is heavily read during normal operation, that performance cost can become noticeable.
Double-Checked Locking A more efficient thread-safe approach is double-checked locking:
public class AppConfig { private static volatile AppConfig instance; private AppConfig() { } public static AppConfig getInstance() { if (instance == null) { synchronized (AppConfig.class) { if (instance == null) { instance = new AppConfig(); } } } return instance; } } This version minimizes locking overhead while still ensuring safe publication. The use of volatile is important because it prevents stale reads and reordering issues.
This is a classic Java pattern for lazy-singleton initialization. It is still widely discussed, but there is usually an even cleaner alternative.
The Best Java Idiom: Initialization-on-Demand Holder The most common production-safe pattern in Java today is the initialization-on-demand holder idiom:
public class AppConfig { private AppConfig() { } private static class Holder { private static final AppConfig INSTANCE = new AppConfig(); } public static AppConfig getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } } This pattern is elegant because:
it is lazy it is thread-safe it avoids synchronization overhead it is simple to understand Java will initialize the nested class only when getInstance() is called. This is often the best choice for a JVM-based service that needs a single instance and no extra ceremony.
This is the kind of implementation I would typically keep in a real enterprise codebase when a true singleton is justified.
When a Singleton Makes Sense A Singleton is appropriate when one instance truly represents a single runtime resource or process-wide policy.
Common examples:
public class MetricsRegistry { private static final MetricsRegistry INSTANCE = new MetricsRegistry(); private final Map<String, Long> counters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); private MetricsRegistry() { } public static MetricsRegistry getInstance() { return INSTANCE; } public void increment(String metricName) { counters.merge(metricName, 1L, Long::sum); } } This is reasonable because a metrics registry is a process-wide concern. A single registry keeps all metrics aggregation centralized.
Another example is a configuration object:
public class EnvironmentConfig { private static class Holder { private static final EnvironmentConfig INSTANCE = new EnvironmentConfig(); } private final String apiBaseUrl; private EnvironmentConfig() { this.apiBaseUrl = System.getenv().getOrDefault("API_BASE_URL", "http://localhost:8080"); } public static EnvironmentConfig getInstance() { return Holder.INSTANCE; } public String getApiBaseUrl() { return apiBaseUrl; } } This is a good example of a singleton representing a true application-wide configuration, not just a convenient holder for random state.
When the Singleton Pattern Becomes a Problem This is where engineering judgment matters.
The Singleton pattern is easy to overuse, and when it is used poorly it creates hidden global state. That introduces several problems:
1. It hides dependencies If a class depends on a singleton, it is not obvious from the constructor what it needs to function.
public class PaymentService { public void processPayment() { PaymentGateway gateway = PaymentGateway.getInstance(); gateway.charge(100); } } This makes the class harder to test and reason about because the dependency is not explicit.
2. It makes unit testing harder Singletons are hard to replace with test doubles. In many codebases, this leads to brittle tests or broad mocking setups.
3. It creates global coupling When many components reach into a singleton, the system becomes more tightly connected than it appears on the surface.
4. It can become a concurrency bottleneck If the singleton owns shared mutable state, everything touches the same object and contention increases.
This does not mean Singletons are always wrong. It means they should be used deliberately and only where the lifecycle semantics justify it.
A Better Alternative in Many Cases: Dependency Injection In modern Java applications, the preferred pattern is often to inject dependencies explicitly rather than reaching into global state.
public class PaymentService { private final PaymentGateway paymentGateway; public PaymentService(PaymentGateway paymentGateway) { this.paymentGateway = paymentGateway; } public void processPayment() { paymentGateway.charge(100); } } This is easier to test, easier to reason about, and more explicit about the object’s runtime relationships.
In a Spring application, this is usually the preferred model. A singleton-like service can still be configured as a bean, but the dependency graph remains explicit.
The Singleton pattern is not inherently bad. It is just often less desirable than explicit wiring when the real requirement is not a global singleton at all.
The Enum Singleton in Java If a class truly needs to be a singleton, the safest Java-specific implementation is often an enum singleton:
public enum SecurityContext { INSTANCE; private final String currentUser = "system"; public String getCurrentUser() { return currentUser; } } This is a strong option because:
the JVM guarantees only one instance exists serialization is handled safely thread safety is built in reflection-based attacks are much harder to execute This is usually the most robust approach when you truly need a singleton in Java.
The trade-off is that an enum is a bit more opinionated. It only makes sense when the singleton is conceptually a fixed, process-wide value or service.
Practical Guidance for Real Teams Here is how I think about the Singleton pattern in production systems:
Use it for true process-wide resources that are conceptually singular. Avoid it for ordinary business objects or convenience access. Prefer explicit dependency injection whenever the object is not truly global. Keep the singleton stateless or carefully controlled when possible. Be careful with mutable shared state. If you use a singleton, choose a thread-safe implementation and document the reason. A good mental model is: a Singleton is an architecture decision, not a coding shortcut.
Final Thoughts The Singleton pattern is one of the clearest examples of a design pattern that is simple to explain and easy to misuse.
Its value is real when you need a single, well-defined runtime authority: a configuration hub, a metrics registry, a process-wide coordination object, or a service that must be globally consistent.
Its risk is equally real when it becomes a hidden global variable in disguise.
That is why the Singleton pattern deserves respect, but not worship.
The right question is not “Can I make this a singleton?” The better question is “Does the system truly require exactly one instance, and does that design improve correctness and maintainability rather than merely reducing typing?”
That is the difference between an intentional design and a convenience hack.
If you want a singleton, implement it carefully. If you do not need one, avoid it. The best Java code is usually the code that makes its dependencies explicit and keeps the system honest.

Design Patterns Are Not a Fancy Acronym. They Are a Professional Discipline. When I review code, the difference between a team that is shipping features and a team that is building durable systems is usually not raw intelligence. It is the discipline of design.
The best engineering teams do not treat design as a luxury. They treat it as a force multiplier.
Design patterns are one of the clearest expressions of that discipline. They are not “pattern matching” for the sake of aesthetics. They are battle-tested ways to structure code so that software is easier to understand, easier to extend, and less likely to collapse under the weight of change.
In enterprise Java systems, where requirements evolve, integrations multiply, and technical debt accumulates quietly over time, patterns matter even more. A team that understands design patterns usually writes software that is more coherent, easier to test, and less likely to require a rewrite after the second or third major release.
The real question is not whether you know the names of the patterns. The question is whether you know when to apply them and whether you can apply them without over-engineering.
That is the difference between a clever engineer and a principal engineer.
Why Design Patterns Matter in Software Engineering Software engineering is fundamentally about managing complexity.
Every system starts with a clean idea and a plausible code path. Then real life arrives: new requirements, changing data sources, regulatory constraints, third-party APIs, performance problems, and the inevitable pressure to patch quickly. That is when complexity becomes the real adversary.
Design patterns help by giving us a vocabulary for recurring problems.
Instead of every developer inventing a custom solution from scratch, a mature team can say:
“This is a strategy problem.” “This is a factory problem.” “This is a decorator problem.” “This is an observer problem.” That shared language reduces ambiguity. It also helps teams avoid the anti-pattern of doing everything ad hoc and then pretending the lack of structure is a feature.
A pattern is valuable when it does three things well:
It makes intent explicit. It reduces accidental complexity. It supports extensibility without destroying cohesion. Consider a common enterprise scenario: payment processing. If every service in the system calculates fees, builds different gateway clients, and directly couples to vendor classes, the code will become brittle. When a new payment method arrives, the team will edit three or four unrelated classes and the risk of bugs goes up dramatically.
That is exactly the kind of problem design patterns are designed to solve.
The Gang of Four: The Foundation of Modern Object-Oriented Design The book most engineers mean when they say “design patterns” is Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software, published in 1994 by Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson, and John Vlissides — collectively known as the Gang of Four, or GoF.
The book changed software engineering by codifying what experienced designers already knew: many object-oriented problems recur, and reusable solutions can be captured and taught.
The GoF did not invent the idea of design patterns in the abstract, but they gave the practice a common language and a durable framework. They organized patterns into three categories:
1. Creational patterns These focus on object creation. They help decouple a system from the concrete classes it creates.
Typical examples:
Factory Method Abstract Factory Builder Singleton Prototype Why they matter:
They control how objects are created. They reduce coupling to constructors and concrete implementations. They make it easier to swap implementations without rewriting the system. 2. Structural patterns These explain how classes and objects compose to form larger structures.
Typical examples:
Adapter Bridge Composite Decorator Facade Flyweight Proxy Why they matter:
They help combine components in a stable way. They let systems evolve without forcing a redesign of the whole object graph. They isolate change behind well-defined boundaries. 3. Behavioral patterns These define communication and responsibility between objects.
Typical examples:
Strategy Observer Command Iterator State Template Method Visitor Why they matter:
They simplify interactions between collaborators. They help distribute responsibilities without producing a tangled object graph. They improve system flexibility when user behavior or workflow changes. The GoF’s core point is simple but powerful: software design is not only about data structures. It is also about the relationships between objects and the responsibilities those objects hold.
That is the real value of the book: it gives engineers a disciplined vocabulary for describing and solving recurring architecture problems.
A Practical Summary of the GoF Book If I had to reduce the book to a single sentence, it would be this:
“Design patterns are reusable object-oriented solutions to recurring design problems, expressed in terms of responsibilities, interactions, and trade-offs.”
This is important because patterns are not magical formulas. They are ways of thinking.
The GoF explicitly frames patterns in terms of:
the problem being solved, the context in which it arises, the participants involved, the consequences of the solution, and the trade-offs you accept. That last point matters more than most people realize. Every pattern makes some aspects of the system easier while making other things more complex. There is no free lunch in architecture.
For example:
A Factory pattern hides construction details, but adds another layer of indirection. A Strategy pattern enables runtime flexibility, but requires a consistent interface across algorithms. A Decorator pattern keeps things open for extension, but can make debugging harder when many wrappers exist. A Singleton pattern is simple to reason about in some cases, but it often becomes a global variable in disguise. The GoF’s value is not that every pattern must be used everywhere. Their value is that they give you a mental model for recognizing the right tool for the right problem.
Good engineers do not memorize patterns. They understand the forces behind them.
The Relationship Between SOLID and Design Patterns If design patterns are the “how,” then SOLID is the “why.”
SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles introduced by Robert C. Martin, and it maps directly to the realities that patterns address.
The five principles are:
Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) A class should have one reason to change.
This principle is the foundation of good cohesion. If a class owns too many responsibilities, it becomes a fragile dependency magnet.
A classic sign of SRP violation is a service that handles validation, persistence, workflow orchestration, and email notifications all in one class.
public class OrderService { public void placeOrder(Order order) { validate(order); save(order); sendConfirmationEmail(order); publishOrderCreatedEvent(order); } private void validate(Order order) { } private void save(Order order) { } private void sendConfirmationEmail(Order order) { } private void publishOrderCreatedEvent(Order order) { } } This class has multiple reasons to change. If email rules change, if persistence changes, or if the order validation model changes, this one class has to be reopened repeatedly.
A more disciplined design splits responsibilities across components.
public class OrderService { private final OrderValidator validator; private final OrderRepository repository; private final OrderNotifier notifier; public OrderService(OrderValidator validator, OrderRepository repository, OrderNotifier notifier) { this.validator = validator; this.repository = repository; this.notifier = notifier; } public void placeOrder(Order order) { validator.validate(order); repository.save(order); notifier.sendConfirmation(order); } } This is not just cleaner code. It is more stable code.
Open/Closed Principle (OCP) Software entities should be open for extension and closed for modification.
This is one of the most important ideas behind patterns like Strategy, Decorator, and Factory. You want to add behavior by introducing new types, not by changing old code in place.
public interface ShippingStrategy { double calculateCost(Order order); } public class GroundShipping implements ShippingStrategy { @Override public double calculateCost(Order order) { return 12.00; } } public class ExpressShipping implements ShippingStrategy { @Override public double calculateCost(Order order) { return 25.00; } } Now the shipping logic can vary without rewriting the order flow:
public class OrderService { private final ShippingStrategy shippingStrategy; public OrderService(ShippingStrategy shippingStrategy) { this.shippingStrategy = shippingStrategy; } public double calculateTotal(Order order) { return order.getSubtotal() + shippingStrategy.calculateCost(order); } } This is an example of the Strategy pattern in action. The behavior is extended by new implementations, not by modifying the order service itself.
Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without breaking the system.
This principle matters whenever we rely on polymorphism. If a subtype violates the expectations of the parent type, the design becomes brittle and surprising.
A classic violation would be using a Square that breaks Rectangle expectations, or a PaymentGateway implementation that throws on refund() because it was only designed for charges.
public interface PaymentGateway { void charge(BigDecimal amount); void refund(BigDecimal amount); } public class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { @Override public void charge(BigDecimal amount) { // charge with Stripe API } @Override public void refund(BigDecimal amount) { // refund with Stripe API } } If a different implementation is added, it should honor the same contract. If it cannot, the abstraction is wrong or too broad.
Interface Segregation Principle (ISP) Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use.
This leads to small, focused interfaces instead of one “god” interface with dozens of methods.
public interface UserRepository { User findById(String id); void save(User user); } public interface AuditRepository { void recordAudit(AuditEvent event); } Rather than a single bloated interface like UserService and AuditService combined, the design keeps contracts specialized. This reduces coupling and makes implementation easier to maintain.
Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) Depend on abstractions, not concretions.
This principle is critical for enterprise Java systems and is deeply connected to design patterns like Factory, Dependency Injection, and Strategy.
public interface NotificationSender { void send(String message); } public class EmailNotificationSender implements NotificationSender { @Override public void send(String message) { System.out.println("Sending email: " + message); } } Then the client depends on the abstraction:
public class AccountService { private final NotificationSender notificationSender; public AccountService(NotificationSender notificationSender) { this.notificationSender = notificationSender; } public void register(String email) { // business logic notificationSender.send("Welcome!"); } } This is a cleaner design because the service is not hardwired to a specific email provider or implementation detail.
How SOLID Relates to Design Patterns The easiest way to think about this is:
SOLID gives you the principles. Design patterns give you the application of those principles in recurring situations. The relationship is not accidental. Patterns often emerge because a team is trying to satisfy one or more SOLID goals.
Take Strategy as an example.
The goal is to keep behavior extensible and avoid hardcoding logic into a central class. That aligns directly with OCP and DIP. The pattern is the structural expression of those principles in a reusable form.
Similarly:
Factory and Abstract Factory are solutions to construction problems that reduce direct dependency on concrete classes. Decorator is a natural expression of OCP: extend behavior without changing the original type. Observer is a way to manage change propagation while keeping coupling manageable. Facade simplifies a complex system and clarifies boundaries, helping reduce SRP violations from a consumer’s perspective. Adapter helps integrate incompatible interfaces without redesigning the world. A simple rule of thumb:
If SOLID is the architectural compass, design patterns are the map. They guide implementation choices without replacing judgment.
This is where many engineers stumble: they confuse “knowing patterns” with “designing well.” A pattern is not a substitute for thinking. It is a tool to avoid poor thinking.
Patterns Are a Language, Not a Religion I have seen teams over-apply patterns. They create abstract factories for everything, decorate every object, and turn a simple service into a cathedral of indirection.
That is not engineering. It is pattern worship without judgment.
The right standard is not “Do I know a pattern for this?” The right standard is “Does this design reduce uncertainty and clarify intent in a way that helps the next engineer safely evolve the code?”
The best use of design patterns is selective and pragmatic:
Use them where the problem is recurring and the cost of a custom solution is high. Keep the abstraction honest and narrow. Prefer clear behavior over theoretical elegance. Favor simplicity until complexity demonstrates it is necessary. A good design does not impress by showing off. It demonstrates restraint, clarity, and resilience under change.
That is why the GoF patterns endure. They are not just intellectual curiosities. They are practical, repeatable solutions to ordinary engineering problems.
And their value is multiplied when they are grounded in SOLID principles. Patterns without principles become decorative. Principles without patterns become vague philosophy. Together, they form a disciplined approach to building software that can evolve without falling apart.
Final Thoughts Design patterns matter because software engineering is not just about writing code that works once. It is about writing code that remains understandable, flexible, and correct as the system grows.
The Gang of Four distilled the experience of generations of software designers into a toolkit for recurring problems. SOLID principles gave us the underlying guidance for keeping systems coherent and maintainable. Together, they define how thoughtful engineers create software that scales beyond the original sprint.
If you are building in Java, or any language for that matter, the practical takeaway is straightforward:
Notice the recurring design problems. Choose the right pattern for the forces at play. Keep the design aligned with SOLID principles. Refactor toward clarity, not complexity. That is how we move from writing code to engineering systems.
And that is the difference between building features and building software that lasts.
